items.title: How to Have Enough: Wendell Berry on Creativity and Love
items.description: “Enough is so vast a sweetness, I suppose it never occurs, only pathetic counterfeits,” Emily Dickinson sighed in one of her love letters to Susan an epoch before Kurt Vonnegut, in a short and lovely poem, distilled happiness to the knowledge that you have enough. items.title: How We Render Reality: Attention as an Instrument of Love
items.description: "Since our consciousness plays some part in what comes into being, the play of attention can both create and destroy, but it never leaves its object unchanged."

items.title: Matter, Memory, and the Paradox of Perception: Henri Bergson on How to See Reality
items.description: In 1896, decades before Santiago Ramón y Cajal pioneered neuroscience, more than a century before Oliver Sacks showed us how perception phosphoresces in the 100 milliseconds between the world and us, half a lifetime before he was awarded the Nobel Prize, the polymathic French philosopher Henri Bergson (October 18, 1859–January 4, 1941) aimed his uncommon mind at “the threefold problem of matter, consciousness, and their relation” in what became Matter and Memory (public library | public domain)

items.title: A Parliament of Owls and a Murder of Crows: How a Forgotten Medieval Woman Gave Groups of Birds Their Strange Names, with Wondrous Vintage Illustrations by Brian Wildsmith
items.description: Language is an instrument of great precision and poignancy — our best tool for telling each other what the world is and what we are, for conveying the blueness of blue and the wonder of being alive. But it is also a thing of great pliancy and creativity — a living reminder that how we name things changes what we see, changes the seer. (This, of course, is why we have poetry.) items.title: How Do We Know What We Want: Milan Kundera on the Central Ambivalences of Life and Love
items.description: "We can never know what to want, because, living only one life, we can neither compare it with our previous lives nor perfect it in our lives to come... We live everything as it comes, without warning."

items.title: The Bird in You, the World in You, and the Art of Trusting Time: Ceramics, Serpentine, and How to Get Over Heartbreak
items.description: One December afternoon, I arrived in Patagonia with a big blue backpack, a small bilingual edition of Pablo Neruda’s love poems, and a broken heart. items.title: The Paradox of Knowing Who You Are and What You Want: Cristina Campo on Fairy Tales, Time, and the Meaning of Maturity
items.description: “If you want your children to be intelligent, read them fairy tales,” Einstein reportedly told one mother who wished for her son to become a scientist. “If you want them to be very intelligent, read them more fairy tales.” Given that the deepest measure of intelligence is a plasticity of being that allows us to navigate uncertainty, given that uncertainty is the pulse-beat of our lives, fairy tales are not — as J.R.R. items.title: The Invention of Zero: How Ancient Mesopotamia Created the Mathematical Concept of Nought and Ancient India Gave It Symbolic Form
items.description: "If you look at zero you see nothing; but look through it and you will see the world."

items.title: The Art of Solitude: Buddhist Scholar and Teacher Stephen Batchelor on Contemplative Practice and Creativity
items.description: "Here lies the paradox of solitude. Look long and hard enough at yourself in isolation and suddenly you will see the rest of humanity staring back."

items.title: A Lei for Your Losses: Joan Didion on the Art of Letting Go
items.description: “We cannot deeply love anything without becoming vulnerable to loss,” Judith Viorst wrote in her defense of life’s necessary losses, “and we cannot become separate people, responsible people, connected people, reflective people without some losing and leaving and letting go.” We know that loving anything or anyone is a contract with loss, and yet we love anyway, our lives a ceaseless osmosis of holding on and letting go, an endless apprenticeship in the art of losing. items.title: The Creative Power of Uncertainty: Polish Poet Wisława Szymborska’s Magnificent Nobel Prize Acceptance Speech
items.description: "Whatever inspiration is, it's born from a continuous ‘I don't know.’"

items.title: Italo Calvino on Reading and Sex
items.description: "Lovers’ reading of each other’s bodies... differs from the reading of written pages in that it is not linear... What makes lovemaking and reading resemble each other most is that within both of them times and spaces open, different from measurable time and space."

items.title: Wendell Berry on Hope, Despair, and the Measure of Effective Protest
items.description: The current of life is charged by the poles of hope and despair. What we make of our hopes and their devastation may be the purest measure of who we are and what we leave behind. Protest is what we call the resistance we launch against our reasons for despair — personal, political, existential. items.title: The Thing Itself: C.S. Lewis on What We Long for in Our Existential Longing
items.description: "...only the scent of a flower we have not found, the echo of a tune we have not heard, news from a country we have never visited."

items.title: The 3 Buddhist Steps to Repairing a Relationship
items.description: "The intention of deep listening and loving speech is to restore communication, because once communication is restored, everything is possible."
